title: How a Browser Draws a Page
summary: See what the browser does with the files it receives: the DOM, the CSSOM, the render tree, layout, paint, and compositing.
intro: The previous lessons followed a page's files across the internet to your browser. This one follows them the rest of the way, from bytes to the picture on your screen. Turning files into that picture is called **rendering**, and it explains things you've surely seen: a page that stays blank while it loads, text that jumps down when a picture arrives, an animation that stutters. You'll see what a browser is made of, how it reads HTML into a tree, how it matches CSS to that tree, how it works out where everything goes and paints it, and how it does it all again each time something changes. You don't need to know HTML or CSS yet. Every line of code is explained as it comes.

steps.title: What a browser is made of
steps.body:
A browser looks like one program: a window with tabs. Inside, it's several programs working together. Knowing which one does what explains why one broken tab doesn't take the others down, why a web page can't read the files on your computer, and why the same page can look a little different in Chrome and in Safari.

## Several programs in one window

A program that's running is called a **process**. Your operating system gives each process its own memory, and no other process can reach into it. Browsers split their work across several processes, so that one failing doesn't bring down the rest. Chrome's are the best known, and the other browsers work much the same way:

- The **browser process** is in charge. It draws the address bar, the tabs, and the buttons around the page, and it decides what every other process is allowed to do.
- A **renderer process** turns one site's files into a page. Each site usually gets its own. When a page crashes, its tab shows an error page, Aw, Snap! in Chrome, and your other tabs carry on.
- The **GPU process** puts pictures on the screen. A **GPU**, or graphics processing unit, is a chip built to draw pixels fast.
- The **network service** fetches everything from the internet: the DNS lookups, the connections, and the HTTP requests from the previous lesson.

```diagram how-browsers-render-processes
Renderers can't reach your files or the network. They ask the browser process.
```

Processes can't share memory, so they talk by sending each other messages. That's called **IPC**, short for inter-process communication. In the diagram, a renderer that needs a file doesn't fetch it itself: it asks the browser process, which has the network service fetch it and passes the bytes back. When the renderer has a picture of the page ready, it goes to the GPU process to be shown.

You can see these processes. In Chrome, open its menu (the three dots at the top right), then More tools, then Task manager. Each row is one process, with how much memory it's using.

## The sandbox and site isolation

A renderer runs code from whatever site you open, and not every site means well. So each renderer runs in a **sandbox**: it can't read your files, turn on your camera, or reach the network by itself. Whatever it needs, it asks the browser process for, and the browser process can say no.

**Site isolation** goes a step further: pages from different sites go in different renderer processes. So even if a page found a way around the browser's other rules, your bank's page wouldn't be in its memory to read.

## Engines

Two parts of a renderer do most of the work:

- A **rendering engine** reads HTML and CSS and draws the page. Chrome, Edge, Opera, and Brave use **Blink**. Safari uses **WebKit**. Firefox uses **Gecko**.
- A **JavaScript engine** runs the page's JavaScript. Chrome and Edge use **V8**, Safari uses **JavaScriptCore**, and Firefox uses **SpiderMonkey**. Node.js, the program you checked with `node --version`, is V8 running on its own, outside any browser.

Three rendering engines means three separate programs reading your page. That's why it pays to check your work in more than one browser, and why a new feature sometimes works in one before the others.

## Who writes the rules

The engines agree with each other because they follow the same written rules, called **standards**, or **specifications** (specs for short). Three groups write the ones you'll use:

- The **WHATWG** writes HTML and the DOM, which the next part explains. Its HTML spec is a Living Standard: it's updated all the time, with no numbered versions.
- The **W3C**, the World Wide Web Consortium, writes CSS.
- **TC39** writes JavaScript, whose official name is ECMAScript. A new edition comes out every year.

The companies that make browsers are members of all three, so a new feature is agreed on before it ships.

## Baseline: does it work everywhere?

Each browser ships new features on its own schedule, so a question you'll ask often is whether a feature works in every browser yet. **Baseline** answers it. It's a label at the top of each feature's page on MDN, the reference site from the previous lesson, and on caniuse.com.

- **Widely available** means the feature has worked in Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari, on computers and on phones, for at least two and a half years. Use it freely.
- **Newly available** means it works in the latest version of all of them. Most visitors have it, but people on older browsers don't.
- **Limited availability** means at least one of them doesn't have it yet.

This course points out anything that isn't Widely available yet when it comes up.

steps.title: Reading HTML into the DOM
steps.body:
An HTML file is only text. Before the browser can style a page or draw it, it reads that text and builds something it can work with, called the DOM. The DOM is what CSS styles and what JavaScript changes, and when a page doesn't look like the HTML you wrote, the DOM is where you look. ## A page to follow This lesson follows one small page all the way to the screen. It's made of two files. Here's `index.html`: ```html Kittens

Kittens

Kittens sleep a lot. ``` Line by line: the first line says this is a modern HTML page. `` holds the name on the browser tab. `<link>` tells the browser to fetch a stylesheet called `style.css` and use it. `<h1>` is the main heading, `<p>` is a paragraph, and `<em>` marks words to stress, which browsers show in italics. A tag with a slash, like `</h1>`, ends what its partner started. The paragraph is never ended, on purpose. The HTML lessons explain every tag here. The second file, `style.css`, holds two CSS rules. The first makes every `h1` purple, and the second sets the size of the text in every paragraph: ```css h1 { color: rebeccapurple; } p { font-size: 20px; } ``` ## From bytes to a tree The file arrives as bytes, and the browser reads them in four steps: 1. **Bytes become characters.** The character set, usually UTF-8, says how letters are stored as bytes. The server's `Content-Type` header can name it, or the page itself can. 2. **Characters become tokens.** The text is cut into pieces that each mean something, called **tokens**: a start tag like `<p>`, an end tag like `</em>`, a run of text, a comment. 3. **Tokens become nodes.** Each tag becomes an **element**, an object that stands for one thing on the page. Each run of text becomes a **text node**. Elements and text nodes are both **nodes**. 4. **Nodes go into a tree.** Each node goes inside the element that was open when it was read. The result is the **DOM**, the Document Object Model: the page as a tree of objects, which the browser keeps in memory while the page is open. Like a family tree, every node has one **parent**, the node it sits inside, and it can have **children**, the nodes inside it. Nodes with the same parent are **siblings**. At the top is the **document**, standing for the whole page, and under it is the `html` element, which holds everything else. ```diagram how-browsers-render-dom-tree The file never mentions html, head, or body. The parser adds them. ``` ## The parser fixes your mistakes The tree in the diagram has three elements the file never mentions: `html`, `head`, and `body`. It also closes the paragraph, which the file never did. The **parser**, the part of the browser that reads HTML, follows rules from the HTML standard for every kind of mistake, so it never gives up on a page. A missing element is added where the rules say it belongs, and an element left open is closed when the next thing can't go inside it. That's kind to beginners, but it has a catch: the page you see is built from the parser's best guess, which might not be what you meant. The HTML lessons show you a tool that finds these mistakes for you. ## It starts before the file has finished The parser doesn't wait for the whole file. It reads bytes as they arrive and builds the tree as it goes, so a long page can show its top while the rest is still on its way. This is called **incremental** parsing. Some things make it stop. When the parser reaches a script, it waits until the script has been fetched and run, because a script can change the page. The JavaScript lessons show how to keep scripts from holding things up. ## The preload scanner While the parser waits, a second, faster reader keeps going. The **preload scanner** skims ahead through the rest of the file, looking only for other files the page will need, like stylesheets, scripts, and pictures, and starts fetching them early. By the time the parser gets to one, it has often already arrived. That's one reason files named plainly in the HTML load sooner than files a script asks for later.

examples.title: What the server sent
examples.prompt: In the Playground, make a folder called `kittens` holding the two files above. Start Python's server in it, as in the earlier lessons, and open `http://localhost:8000/`. Then ask for the page with curl from a second terminal.
examples.explanation: These are the bytes the server sent, exactly as they are in the file: five lines, with no `html`, `head`, or `body`, and a paragraph that's never closed. The browser shows the same thing when you choose **View Page Source**: right-click the page and pick it, or press Ctrl and U (Command, Option, and U on a Mac). The source is always what arrived, before the parser has touched it. Python's server also printed two request lines in the Playground's terminal: one for `/`, and one for `/style.css`, which the browser asked for when it read the `link`.

examples.title: What the browser built
examples.prompt: Now open DevTools on the same page and choose the **Elements** tab. Click each small triangle to open the element beside it. With every one open, it reads like this.
examples.explanation: The Elements tab shows the DOM, not your file. The `html`, `head`, and `body` elements are there, with the title and the stylesheet link sorted into the `head` and the rest into the `body`. The paragraph has an end tag now. Inside it, the words in quotes are its text nodes: one before the `em`, and one after it, holding the full stop. Each line you click in the Elements tab is one node, and the page highlights the part that node draws. When a page looks wrong, this is where to start: compare the tree with what you meant to write.

steps.title: Styles and the render tree
steps.body:
The DOM says what's on a page, but nothing about how it looks. Next, the browser matches every CSS rule to the elements it applies to, then decides what will actually be drawn. This step is also why a page can stay blank while a stylesheet loads, so it's worth knowing what goes on in it.

## Stylesheets become the CSSOM

The first lesson showed that a CSS rule picks things on the page and says how they should look. In `p { font-size: 20px; }`, the `p` is the **selector**: it picks every paragraph. Inside the curly braces, `font-size: 20px` is a **declaration**. It names a **property**, the thing to set, then a colon, then the property's **value**.

The browser reads each stylesheet the way it reads HTML, from bytes to tokens, and builds the **CSSOM**, the CSS Object Model. It holds every rule from every stylesheet, arranged so the browser can quickly find the ones that apply to any element.

One stylesheet is always there, though you never wrote it. Every browser has its own default styles, called the **user agent stylesheet** (user agent is the formal name for a browser). It's what makes an `h1` big and bold, and what puts space above and below each paragraph. Your rules go on top of it, which is why a page with no CSS at all still has big headings.

## Style calculation

Next, for every element in the DOM, the browser works out the final value of every CSS property. This is **style calculation**, and it has three jobs:

- **Match.** Find every rule whose selector picks this element.
- **Settle conflicts.** When two rules set the same property on the same element, decide which one wins. The rules for deciding are called the **cascade**, and the CSS lessons cover them.
- **Fill in the rest.** Some properties pass down from an element to the ones inside it, which is called **inheritance**. Text size does: the `em` in the kittens page is 20px, like the paragraph around it, though no rule picks the `em`. Anything still unset gets a default value.

What comes out, for each element, is its **computed style**: a value for every one of the several hundred CSS properties. You can see it. In the Elements tab of DevTools, click an element, then open the **Computed** pane beside the tree.

## The render tree

Now the browser builds the **render tree**: the parts of the DOM that will actually be drawn, each with its computed style. Chrome calls it the layout tree. The browser walks down the DOM and leaves out two kinds of things:

- The `head`, and everything in it. The title and the stylesheet link describe the page. They aren't things on it.
- Any element whose computed style says `display: none`, along with everything inside it.

```diagram how-browsers-render-render-tree
The render tree keeps only what gets drawn, each part with its computed style.
```

Text nodes stay, since text gets drawn. An element with `visibility: hidden` stays too. It's invisible, but it still takes up its space on the page, so the browser still has to work out how big it is. Think of a row of people in a photo. `display: none` is someone leaving the row, and everyone shuffles along to close the gap. `visibility: hidden` is someone who stays in their spot but can't be seen, so the gap stays.

## Why CSS holds up the first paint

The browser won't draw the page until it has every stylesheet the `head` links to. That's on purpose. If it drew straight away, you'd see the page plain, in the default styles, then watch it jump into shape a moment later. That glitch has a name: a **flash of unstyled content**.

The cost is that CSS is **render-blocking**. While a stylesheet downloads, the screen stays blank, however much HTML has already arrived. One slow stylesheet means a blank page for everyone. That's why sites keep their CSS small and send it fast, which the course covers when you ship your own code.

examples.prompt: Save this as `hidden.html` in your `kittens` folder and open `http://localhost:8000/hidden.html`.

First line

Second line

Third line

Fourth line

Fifth line
examples.explanation: A `<style>` element holds CSS inside the page itself, so this page needs no stylesheet file. `class="gone"` gives the second paragraph a name, and the selector `.gone`, with a dot, picks every element with that class. You'll see First line, Third line, an empty space, then Fifth line. The second paragraph isn't in the render tree, so the third moves up into its place. The fourth is still there, holding its space, but drawn invisibly. Open the Elements tab and both paragraphs are in the DOM. Click each one: the page highlights the fourth paragraph's box, while the second has no box to show.

steps.title: Layout, paint, and compositing
steps.body:
The render tree says what to draw and how it should look, but not where. Three more steps work out where every box goes, what color every pixel is, and how they reach the screen. These steps are where a page spends most of its drawing time, and knowing which one a change sets off is the secret to smooth scrolling and animation.

## Layout: where everything goes

**Layout** works out the **geometry** of everything in the render tree: where each thing sits, and how big it is, in pixels. To the browser, everything on a page is a rectangle, called a **box**, and layout gives every box its size and position.

It starts from the **viewport**, the part of the browser window that shows the page. The `body` takes the viewport's width, less a small margin, and the `h1` takes the body's width. The heading's height comes from the size of its text. The paragraph goes under the heading, and how many lines its text needs depends on how wide it is.

So boxes depend on each other. Make the window narrower, and the paragraph's text wraps onto more lines, the paragraph gets taller, and everything below it moves down. That chain is why layout can be slow on a big page, and why the browser tries to only lay out again the parts that changed. Firefox calls this step **reflow**, and you'll see both words.

DevTools shows layout's work. Hover over an element in the Elements tab, and the page highlights its box, with its width and height.

## Paint: what to draw

**Paint** turns the laid-out boxes into a list of drawing instructions, in the order they'll be drawn: fill the page with white, write Kittens in purple, in big bold letters, at this spot, then write the paragraph's words below it. What sits behind is drawn before what sits in front.

Then comes **raster**, which carries out the list and works out the color of every single pixel. Browsers usually raster on the GPU, which is built for exactly this kind of work.

## Layers and compositing

A browser can split a page into **layers**, like clear plastic sheets stacked on top of each other. The page itself is one layer. Something that moves on its own, like a menu that stays put while you scroll, or a box that's being animated, can get a layer of its own, painted separately.

**Compositing** is the last step. The **compositor** stacks the layers in order, each in its place, to make the finished picture, and the GPU puts it on the screen. The compositor runs separately from the rest of the work, so it can keep going while the rest is busy. When you scroll, much of the work is the compositor sliding layers along, with no new layout or paint at all.

## What a change costs

A change to the page starts this chain at one stage, and every stage after it runs too:

```diagram how-browsers-render-pipeline
The later a change enters the chain, the less work it takes.
```

- A change to a size or a position, like `width`, `margin`, or `font-size`, runs **layout**, then paint, then compositing. That's the most work.
- A change to looks alone, like `color` or `background`, skips layout, since nothing moved. It runs paint and compositing.
- A change to `transform`, which moves, turns, or scales a box as it's drawn, or to `opacity`, how see-through it is, can skip both when the box has its own layer. The compositor redraws it from the layer it already has.

That's why animations that stay smooth move things with `transform` and fade them with `opacity`. The CSS lessons come back to it.

## See paint happen

DevTools can flash every area it repaints. Open DevTools and press Ctrl, Shift, and P (Command, Shift, and P on a Mac) to open its command menu. Type Rendering, choose Show Rendering, and tick **Paint flashing**. Now scroll a page, or move your pointer over its links. Each green flash is an area being painted again.

examples.title: Three changes, three costs
examples.prompt: Three CSS rules for an element with the class `banner`. Each one changes something different, so each one costs the browser a different amount of work.
examples.explanation: The first rule adds 40 pixels of space above the banner. That changes where the banner sits, and where everything after it sits, so the browser runs layout, paint, and compositing. The second changes the background to gold. Nothing moves, so it skips layout and runs paint and compositing. The third slides the banner 40 pixels down as it's drawn and makes it half see-through. The banner's box doesn't move as far as layout is concerned, so nothing around it shifts. When the banner has its own layer, the compositor handles both changes alone. Once is cheap either way. The difference shows when a change happens on every frame, as it does in an animation.

steps.title: Rendering again, many times a second
steps.body:
Rendering doesn't happen only once, when a page loads. Every time something changes, the browser renders again. Most of what makes a page feel quick or sluggish happens here, long after it has loaded, so this part is about doing it again, and fast.

## Every change renders again

After the first render, a page keeps changing. JavaScript adds an item to a list. A button changes color as your pointer moves over it. A picture finishes loading, or a font arrives. You resize the window, or scroll. Each time, the browser runs again the steps the change needs: style calculation for what changed, then layout, paint, and compositing, as far down the chain as the change reaches.

Three words describe how much runs again:

- **Reflow**, or re-layout: layout runs again, and paint and compositing after it.
- **Repaint**: paint and compositing run again, but not layout.
- A **composite-only** update: only compositing runs.

Reflow is the costly one, since moving one box can move everything after it.

A late picture is the everyday example. When the HTML doesn't say how big a picture is, layout gives it no room at first. When it arrives, layout runs again and makes room for it, and the text you were reading jumps down. That jump is called a **layout shift**. The HTML lessons show the two attributes that prevent it.

## Frames

A screen shows a new picture many times a second: 60 times on most screens, and 120 on many newer phones and laptops. Each picture is a **frame**. The browser tries to have a new frame ready in time for each one.

At 60 a second, that leaves 1,000 milliseconds divided by 60, about 16 milliseconds per frame, for everything: running JavaScript, style, layout, paint, and compositing. The browser needs some of that time for its own work, so a page's code gets about 10 milliseconds a frame.

## Jank

When a frame isn't ready in time, the screen shows the old one again. That's a **dropped frame**. One now and then, nobody notices. Several in a row look like a stutter: a scroll that sticks, or an animation that jerks. People call that **jank**.

```diagram how-browsers-render-frames
A long task holds the main thread, so the frames due while it runs never come.
```

The usual cause is the **main thread**. A **thread** is one line of work inside a process, doing one thing after another, and a renderer does most of its work on one main thread: JavaScript, style, layout, and paint all take turns there. While a piece of JavaScript runs, nothing else on the main thread can, so no new frames are made and clicks and key presses go unanswered. Work that holds the main thread for more than 50 milliseconds is called a **long task**.

In the diagram, frames 1 to 3 are ready on time. Then a long task holds the main thread for about 60 milliseconds. The three frames due while it runs are dropped, and the screen keeps showing frame 3 until the task ends and frame 4 can finally be made.

The compositor runs on a thread of its own. That's why a page can often still scroll while its JavaScript is busy, even though nothing you click responds, and why the transform animations from the previous part keep going too.

## Finding it

The **Performance** panel in DevTools records everything the browser does for a few seconds. Press record, scroll or click around, then stop. It shows each frame, and marks each long task with a red corner. The course comes back to it when you make your own pages fast.

## The other meaning of rendering

You'll hear rendering used for something else, too: making the HTML. A server can **render** a page, putting its HTML together before sending it, which is the generated response from the lesson on servers. The React course covers that meaning. In this lesson, rendering is always the browser's work: turning files into pixels.

examples.title: A smooth box and a stuck one
examples.prompt: Save this as `jank.html` in your `kittens` folder and open it. You don't need to follow the CSS or the script yet. Watch the two squares, then press the button.
examples.explanation: Both squares slide back and forth. The top one moves with `transform`, and the bottom one with `margin-left`, a property that changes layout. Pressing the button runs a script that keeps the main thread busy for three seconds, doing nothing but checking the clock: one very long task. The bottom square freezes, because each step of its slide needs layout, and layout runs on the main thread. The top square keeps sliding, because the compositor moves its layer on its own thread. Try to select some text or press the button again during those three seconds: nothing happens until the task ends.

steps.title: The browser as a platform
steps.body:
The code in a web page does a lot: it changes the page, talks to servers, and remembers things. Surprisingly little of that is JavaScript itself. Most of it comes from the browser. Knowing which is which tells you where to look things up, and why code that works in a page can fail in Node.js, and the other way round.

## The language, and what's around it

JavaScript, the language TC39 writes, is small on its own. It has values like numbers and text, variables to keep them in, functions, decisions, and loops. That's about it. It knows nothing about pages, screens, or networks.

Everything else comes from the program the JavaScript engine runs inside, called its **host**. The host gives JavaScript a set of ready-made things it can use. A set like that is called an **API**, an Application Programming Interface: a list of named things one program offers to another, and what each one does when it's used. The APIs a browser offers are called **Web APIs**.

```diagram how-browsers-render-web-apis
The engine runs the language. The Web APIs around it come from the browser.
```

## The map

These are the Web APIs you'll use most:

| Web API | What it gives your code |
|---|---|
| DOM | the page's tree: find elements, change them, and react to clicks and typing |
| CSSOM | the page's styles, and any element's computed style |
| Fetch | HTTP requests to servers, sent from code without loading a new page |
| Storage | small amounts of information kept in the browser between visits |
| History | a new address in the address bar without loading a new page |
| Timers | code that runs later, or again and again |
| Workers | code that runs on another thread, away from the main one |
| Media | sound, video, the camera, and the microphone |

Each one shows up in code as a name you can use. `document` is the DOM, `fetch` sends a request, `localStorage` is one kind of storage, and `setTimeout` is a timer. None of them is part of the JavaScript language. The JavaScript lessons in this course teach the language first, then the DOM, then fetch, storage, history, timers, and workers.

## Same language, another host

Node.js is a host too, with the same V8 engine inside as Chrome. But it runs programs on your computer, not pages in a tab, so it offers other APIs: reading and writing files, starting servers, and talking to the operating system. There's no page, so there's no `document`. A few APIs are useful in both places, so both hosts offer them: `console` for printing, timers like `setTimeout`, and `fetch`.

That's why code that changes a page fails in Node, and why code that reads files from your disk can't run in a page. The sandbox wouldn't allow it anyway. When you look something up on MDN, it tells you which one it is: the JavaScript reference covers the language, and the Web APIs reference covers what the browser adds.

## Who decides when your code runs

The host also decides when your code runs. Most code in a page waits for something: a click, a timer, a server's answer. When that something happens, the browser puts the code that was waiting for it in a queue. A loop on the main thread, called the **event loop**, takes the waiting pieces of code out one at a time and runs them, in between making frames.

It's the same main thread as in the previous part, which is why a long task freezes the page: until it ends, the event loop can't run anything else, and no frames get made. The JavaScript lessons take the event loop apart, and show how to keep it moving.

First comes the page itself. The next lesson starts on HTML, the elements every DOM is built from.

examples.title: The same question in two hosts
examples.prompt: Ask Node.js which of these names it knows. Run this in the Playground's terminal. `typeof` asks what kind of thing a name is.
examples.code: node -e "console.log(typeof document, typeof setTimeout, typeof fetch)"
examples.explanation: `node -e` runs the JavaScript in quotes straight away, without a file. It prints one word for each name. `document` is `undefined`: Node has no page, so it has no DOM. `setTimeout` and `fetch` are both `function`, things you can call, because Node offers them as well as browsers do. Now open DevTools on any page, choose the **Console** tab, type `typeof document`, and press Enter. The browser answers `'object'`: in a page, `document` is the DOM. The language is the same in both places. What changes is what each host puts around it.

recap:
- A browser is several processes: the browser process in charge, a sandboxed renderer for each site, a GPU process, and a network service.
- Blink, WebKit, and Gecko draw pages, V8, JavaScriptCore, and SpiderMonkey run JavaScript, and they all follow the same standards.
- Baseline says whether a feature works in every major browser, and Widely available means it's safe to use.
- The parser turns HTML into the DOM, a tree of nodes, fixing mistakes and starting before the file has finished arriving.
- CSS becomes the CSSOM, every element gets a computed style, and the render tree keeps only what gets drawn.
- Layout gives each box its size and place, paint and raster turn boxes into pixels, and compositing stacks the layers.
- Every change renders again, and at 60 frames a second each frame has about 16 ms, so long tasks cause jank.
- The DOM, fetch, storage, and timers are Web APIs the browser adds, not part of the JavaScript language.
